item.title: Why These Giant Storage Tanks Increasingly Hold Very Little Oil
item.description:
Hundreds of steel tanks several stories tall rise like giant bales of hay from the plains. They make up the largest private oil storage site in the United States, and, after six months of war, they are close to the emptiest they have been in recent years.

Companies drew down the oil stashed here in central Oklahoma as energy prices surged in recent months.

The world is getting by on other buffers, but those will last only so long.

That timeline depends on the how the war between the United States and Iran evolves, but one thing is clear: Policymakers and oil companies the world over are eager to build or expand stockpiles to insulate themselves from the next energy shock.

Among them are Persian Gulf oil producers, such as Saudi Arabia, that want to stockpile more oil overseas, far from maritime choke points like the Strait of Hormuz. “Producers need to invest in storage that is not necessarily in their country,” said Amos Hochstein, a senior adviser on energy and foreign policy in the Biden administration.

The challenge is different in the United States, which has ample oil storage capacity but dwindling inventory. The federal government has been steadily depleting its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which recently fell to its lowest levels since 1982.

Note: Data as of August 21.

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Leanne Abraham/The New York Times

Most private companies have little incentive to hold on to oil. That is because oil is worth more today than traders believe it will be several months from now. As a result, many of the storage tanks here, outside the small town of Cushing, Okla., contain little more than what is needed to keep systems running.

A recent tour of these tank farms showed how these private stockpiles work.

Cushing was one of America’s early oil boomtowns. The area’s first commercial oil well was drilled in 1912, and dozens of refineries were built to process that oil into fuels. New pipelines connected Cushing to markets as far as Indiana in the 1920s.

Production, however, collapsed almost as quickly as it had started. But Cushing was not completely forlorn. The town’s central location and network of pipelines made it an increasingly attractive place to store and trade oil.

The New York Mercantile Exchange chose the town as the trading hub for a new oil contract, West Texas Intermediate, which debuted in 1983 and became the most important price for oil produced in the United States.

“It provided the best access to the refining base in the United States at the time,” said Peter Keavey, global head of energy for CME Group, which operates that exchange.

Today, dozens of pipelines meet in Cushing, connecting oil fields in Canada and Wyoming to refineries in the Midwest and Texas, according to Novi Labs, an energy research firm.

“Without it, getting where you wanted to go would take so much more planning and time and cost,” said Sarah Harris, a director of operations for Oneok, which is based in nearby Tulsa and operates one of the biggest local storage systems.

Some of Oneok’s tanks are so big that they can hold enough oil to power tens of thousands of cars and trucks for a year. When prices are such that oil is worth more in the future, companies use that space to store oil. Early in the Covid-19 pandemic, Cushing’s storage tanks filled up as demand for fuel collapsed during lockdowns, sending U.S. oil prices briefly below zero.

The opposite dynamic has been playing out this year. Oil is scarce and in relatively high demand, but most traders expect that those conditions will eventually end. Regardless of what happens to the Strait of Hormuz, the global oil industry will increase the supply of fuel, the world will learn to live with less, or some combination of the two will happen, the thinking goes.

Cushing’s tank farms held 22 million barrels as of late August, just above minimum operating levels, according to the Energy Information Administration. Removing much more oil could damage equipment, like the steel roofs that float atop the oil or the mixers that blend it the way a KitchenAid machine might a batch of cookie dough.

The oil continues to flow, however, with Cushing acting like a brief rest stop on the way to refineries and ports.

Similar concepts apply to the federal oil stockpile. Analysts disagree about how low U.S. reserves can safely fall, but the government cannot remove all of the oil without risking damage to the underground salt caverns that hold it in Texas and Louisiana.

For now, the world has access to enough oil that prices remain well below the highs seen early in the war. The bigger constraint is that there are not enough refineries to turn the oil into gasoline and other fuels. On Thursday, average U.S. diesel prices were just 7 cents below this year’s peak, according to the AAA motor club.

The longer the war drags on, the more fragile the market is becoming.

item.title: Trump Says U.S. Has Deal for Control of Large Share of Venezuela’s Oil
item.description:
President Trump said late Friday that the United States had struck a deal to take majority control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

Any effort by the federal government to take a stake in another country’s oil fields would be highly unusual. It was not immediately clear what such an arrangement would look like or what Venezuela’s government might have agreed to.

Mr. Trump said in a social media post that the deal involved “a partnership with private business” and would give the United States control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. That is almost as much as all of the proven reserves in the United States, which is the world’s biggest oil producer.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were involved in the negotiations, the president said. Venezuela’s government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Trump administration has made Venezuela’s oil central to its campaign to expand U.S. influence over energy in the Western Hemisphere, where rising production has helped blunt the loss of oil coming out of the Middle East over the past six months because of the Iran war.

Previous U.S. leaders often shied away from any suggestion that gaining control of another country’s natural resources was a primary objective of U.S. military and foreign policy, wary of the international backlash. But President Trump and some of his top advisers have made it clear that oil is an important part of their foray into Venezuela.

Even before the United States removed Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, from power in January, American officials bluntly claimed that the United States had created Venezuela’s oil industry and that the country’s government had effectively stolen U.S. oil fields through nationalizations.

Unlike most other big oil powers, however, the United States does not have a national oil company.

Mr. Trump made his announcement on Friday as Chevron, the second-largest U.S. oil company, was in advanced talks to significantly expand its operations in Venezuela, according to people familiar with the negotiations between the oil company and Venezuelan officials. That deal could be announced as early as next week.

Any new investment by Chevron, the only American company with a major presence in Venezuela, would bolster the country’s efforts to revitalize its ailing oil industry and struggling economy.

Chevron’s negotiations over new investments in Venezuela were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal.

Several other U.S. oil companies have also been pursuing opportunities in the South American country, though much of what has come to fruition so far this year has been preliminary or relatively small.

The negotiations point to the major shift underway in the energy landscape of Venezuela, which is thought to have the world’s largest oil reserves. Maintaining domestic control over natural resources has shaped the country’s politics for decades, and many Venezuelans view oil as a birthright and a cornerstone of national identity.

Under U.S. pressure just weeks after the capture of Mr. Maduro, Venezuela’s National Assembly approved an overhaul of legislation governing its oil industry, granting foreign oil companies greater control over their operations in the country. This move reversed much of Venezuela’s nationalization of oil projects in 2007 and opened the way for Chevron to expand its foothold.

The nationalization had been a pillar of Chavismo, the political movement created by Hugo Chávez, Mr. Maduro’s predecessor, which wielded control over Venezuela until this year.

Mr. Maduro’s successor, Delcy Rodríguez, facing U.S. threats that she could meet a similar fate, has been much more open to working with the U.S. government and frequently talks to and meets with top Trump administration officials.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Treasury Bars Some Reporters From G20 Finance Meeting
item.description:
When leaders from the world’s most powerful countries gather next week for the Group of 20 finance meeting in Asheville, N.C., they will be joined by throngs of journalists from newsrooms around the globe.

Missing from among them, though, will be several reporters from three of the largest newsrooms in the United States.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has not granted credentials to individual reporters for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg News to cover the event, which will draw finance ministers and central bank governors from the world’s biggest economies.

Alan Rappeport, an economic policy reporter who reports on the Treasury Department for The Times, has been excluded from the meeting. Since he began covering the department in 2017, he has attended nearly a dozen G7 and G20 meetings in person.

Matt Grossman, an economics reporter for The Wall Street Journal, was also denied a credential. A spokesman for The Journal declined to comment.

Nicole Taylor, a spokeswoman for The Times, said in a statement that the decision was “not just another disturbing effort by the administration to undermine independent journalism, but a blatant attempt to evade public scrutiny.”

“With the war in Iran, sanctions, the bond markets and inflation on the agenda for the G20 finance ministers, the stakes of this gathering are significant for the global economy and the American people,” the statement said.

A spokesman for the Treasury Department said in a statement that the department would be welcoming “nearly 300 members of the media from approximately a dozen countries,” including reporters from NPR, The Washington Post and Al Jazeera.

“Secretary Bessent will participate in numerous media engagements throughout the event, including one-on-one interviews with local and national outlets across the political spectrum,” the spokesman said. “Members of the media will have a high level of access to policymakers throughout the event, and with that access comes a responsibility to report factual information consistent with established journalistic standards.”

The Treasury spokesman added that a reporter from The Times would be in attendance. The department granted a credential to Jim Tankersley, the Times’s Berlin bureau chief who reports on Germany and other parts of Europe.

Dick Stevenson, The Times’s Washington bureau chief, sent a letter to the Treasury Department on Thursday asking officials there to reconsider the decision not to credential Mr. Rappeport, a Times spokesman said. So far, they have not reversed their decision.

The decision to exclude individual reporters is the latest example of the Trump administration restricting access to certain journalists.

Last year, the Pentagon imposed a restrictive press policy that prompted dozens of journalists from mainstream publications to surrender their press badges in protest. The Times sued the Pentagon, arguing that the new policy violated the First Amendment, and a judge later ruled that it the was unconstitutional.

item.title: Pennsylvania Gambling Addicts Hope That ‘Skill Games’ Will Go Bust
item.description:
Driving home on a recent Friday after another monotonous week of installing drywall, David Peck passed by the sole gas station in Millheim, Pa., and felt a familiar urge.

The front of the Millheim Food Mart, the convenience store attached to the gas station, houses six video screen kiosks, each matched with a swiveling bar chair. With just $8 in his pocket, Mr. Peck, 46, stopped in the store and slipped the money into one of the machines.

His $8 was converted into 800 points and he pressed a button on the kiosk to make colorful icons fall into a tic-tac-toe-like grid. The game was called “Lucky Leprechaun” and the icons were kitschy symbols of luck: four-leaf clovers, golden horseshoes, white rabbits, pots of gold, leprechauns. Each time three of the same icons lined up in a row, points accumulated.

The kiosk looked like a slot machine. It acted like a slot machine. But its designer had carefully implemented one feature that, it argued, would exempt the kiosk from being considered a gambling device: If players lose a spin, they have the option to switch to a different game to win back their points.

These games are based on a skill, like remembering patterns, rather than luck. But they can be tedious, and many players choose not to try to win their points — and money — back.

Because this choice exists, the kiosks are known as “skill games” and were long considered legal in Pennsylvania, allowing them to bypass the state’s regulations on gambling. But a recent ruling by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reclassified the games as a form of gambling, forcing lawmakers to decide how to regulate them.

Pennsylvania has amassed between 70,000 and 100,000 of the games, according to the state Gaming Control Board. They can be found in convenience stores, bars, beer distributors, grocery stores, vape and tobacco shops and even laundromats. These outlets have deals to keep a portion of the money lost by players, and some say the revenue and foot traffic is essential to their bottom line.

Mr. Peck played until he lost all his points, and as a consequence, all his money. The entire experience took about 25 minutes.

On other days, Mr. Peck sits in the Millheim Food Mart through cycles of up and down that last hours and end in losses of hundreds of dollars. “I win,” he said. “I win by a lot, but I don’t ever cash out.”

Over one six-month period, he said, he lost $60,000.

States have had varying responses to the skill games that challenge the spirit, if not the letter, of their gambling laws. Illinois and Georgia accommodated them and passed laws to regulate and tax them. Virginia and North Carolina have tried to ban them. In Wisconsin and Texas, they remain in a legal gray zone.

Pace-O-Matic, a company that leads the skill games industry, introduced its kiosks to Pennsylvania in 2013. State police quickly confiscated the machines, and the company sued to reclaim them — a test of the games’ legality. The next year, a state court ruled in favor of Pace-O-Matic, agreeing that the games on the machines were “predominantly” based on skill. Another state court came to the same conclusion in 2023.

The games have frustrated local lawmakers, some of whom have cited safety concerns about machines stuffed with cash in relatively unguarded businesses. In 2020, a robber murdered a convenience store clerk in Hazelton while stealing cash from the store’s skill games. State lawmakers have introduced various proposals to regulate them. Pace-O-Matic spent millions on lobbyists, and none of the bills became law.

The recent ruling by the state supreme court, in June, said that if a device is partially used for gambling, it is a gambling device. Unless lawmakers decide to pass new protections for the games, they become illegal in October.

For Mr. Peck, skill games are the latest in a long line of dependencies. In the last decade, he has kicked cocaine, heroin, alcohol and meth. In 2021, in a bid to get clean, he moved with his wife at the time to Millheim from the Philadelphia area because they didn’t know any drug dealers there.

Mr. Peck said he used drugs to escape anxiety and post-traumatic stress related to childhood trauma that includes sexual abuse. After he achieved chemical sobriety four years ago, skill games became his new way of blocking painful thoughts.

“I am an addict, plain and simple,” he said. “They are my way of escaping everything.”

A few decades of managing dependencies have instilled in him some self-discipline. He sets aside enough money for food, rent, utilities, taxes and support payments to two children who live with their mothers. The rest, he said, “is going into those machines.” Despite earning about $375,000 in his best year, he has no savings.

Josh Ercole, executive director of the Council on Compulsive Gambling of Pennsylvania, said that the nonprofit received about 100 calls per year from people seeking help who list skill games as their most problematic type of gambling.

Mr. Peck said he couldn’t pinpoint why skill games have a unique pull on him. Part of it is their ubiquity. Millheim is a town of 831 people within 1.3 square miles. It has one intersection with a traffic light and at least 16 skill game machines in five locations.

Across from Mr. Peck’s apartment is a lawn and gardening shop called This Is It, though a sign on the exterior advertising “Pennsylvania SKILL Play Here-Win Here!!!!” is more visible than its name.

Jason Tickner, a 26-year-old Millheim native, opened the shop in 2024 with a business partner who owns a landscaping company. He said they had installed the games to maintain profitability during the winter months.

After a licensing fee is paid to Pace-O-Matic, the profits are split between This Is It and Meile Amusements, the owner-operator of the store’s machines. Mr. Tickner said the games accounted for 25 to 30 percent of the store’s revenue.

Mr. Tickner plays skill games casually. They can take him into a “deep, dark hole real quick,” he said. But he doesn’t have any qualms about profiting from them. “I always just say, ‘Gamble responsibly,’” he said.

Doug Sprankle, president of the Pennsylvania Taverns and Players Association, a lobbying and advocacy group, said skill games were “supposed to be ancillary to what you already do, to help keep the lights on, help pay some of the fees around your business and create entertainment.”

Mr. Sprankle is one of the second generation of co-owners of Sprankle’s Neighborhood Markets, a small chain in Western Pennsylvania. Its skill games are meant to sway customers toward Sprankle’s instead of another supermarket, he said.

He compared them to “pool and arcade games of the old days,” adding that “it’s just something to do to pass a little bit of time in between activities.”

During the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, Jennifer Gower felt a dullness she could not quite articulate. She spent most of her time sequestered in the house she shared with her husband and youngest child near Scranton, Pa.

She had casually visited casinos and bought Pennsylvania Lottery tickets, but gambling never created a problem for her until the pandemic. On each grocery run, she began buying scratch-off tickets. Then she discovered casino game apps for her phone. The dopamine loop was irresistible.

“I would wake up in the morning, and as soon as my feet hit the floor, I was reaching for my phone and spinning slot machines online,” she said.

Ms. Gower, 54, declined to disclose her exact gambling losses, though she said they had quickly amounted to “tens of thousands” of dollars and were “very real for a middle-income household.”

The losses eventually spurred her to call 1-800-GAMBLER, the hotline run by the National Council on Problem Gambling, which connected her with online Gamblers Anonymous meetings and a therapist.

Critical to her recovery, she said, was self-exclusion. Like most states, Pennsylvania maintains a registry to which problem gamblers can voluntarily add themselves. Casinos are obligated to bar them from entry, and the Gaming Control Board sends their names to online gambling companies, ordering them to find and delete their accounts. The law is written so that if someone on the list somehow bypasses these roadblocks, gambling businesses can refuse to pay their winnings.

Ms. Gower self-excluded for a year. After it was up, she quickly relapsed. She then chose to self-exclude for life.

She successfully kicked her gambling habit — until, one day, at a gas station convenience store, she noticed a curious area full of skill games. She sat down and inserted a bill. The experience was indistinguishable from gambling, she said. “There’s the same lights. There’s the same noises. There’s the same dopamine rush.”

Because skill games were not considered gambling, self-exclusion did not apply to them.

Ms. Gower began playing them almost daily. She told her family she was running errands. It was easy; the machines were in places where she went for gas or groceries. She realized she was bleeding as much money as she had on casino apps. After an eight-month binge, she quit.

Skill games, she said, “absolutely need to be regulated like any gambling.”

Mike Barley, a public affairs officer for Pace-O-Matic, said the games’ potential effect on compulsive gamblers was “problematic” and “something we’re cognizant of.” He said the company hoped to address the issue when and if states passed regulations on skill games.

Skill games remove physical or psychological barriers between gambling and nongambling spaces, said Carolyn E. Hawley, a professor of rehabilitation counseling at Virginia Commonwealth University and the director of the Virginia Partnership for Gaming and Health.

The “skill game” label and the games’ presence in everyday places lend a deceptive air of banality, Dr. Hawley said. “It minimizes the potential that this could cause harm.”

The machines once saturated Virginia, but the state General Assembly voted to prohibit them in 2020. Enforcement was paused until the state’s Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2023. The games remain slippery. Some businesses have refused to remove them and Pace-O-Matic has responded with a new machine it claims is compliant with Virginia law, again daring vice squads to confiscate it and possibly restarting the cycle where courts and lawmakers figure out how to regulate the kiosks.

There is evidence that, despite the ban, skill games are enticing more problem gamblers in Virginia. In the Virginia Partnership for Gaming and Health’s annual survey of people referred to its program for help, 4 percent listed skill games as their primary form of gambling in 2024. The number grew to 10 percent in 2025.

In Pennsylvania, the Supreme Court essentially gave lawmakers a choice: pass a law addressing skill games by Oct. 13 or they become illegal.

State Senator Jay Costa, the Senate Democratic leader, said that lawmakers were trying to hash out a plan. He said he did not see a distinction between skill games and slot machines, but he said he thought the state’s best option now was to tax and regulate them.

For now, businesses are keeping the machines until they are forced to remove them.

Mr. Peck is unsure when and if he will walk away. The best scenario for him is that the latest court ruling goes unaddressed and skill games become illegal in Pennsylvania. He thinks he would quit gambling for the most part.

A few times already, it seemed as though he was finished with skill games. After the end of his marriage, he abstained for three months. Whenever he needed gas or cigarettes, he kept a map in his mind of places that did not have them. But he found himself back in the Food Mart’s swivel chairs. (The store’s owner did not respond to requests for comment.)

He is not sure he can quit another addiction. Each time the process seems to take a bit of some exhaustible force within him, he said.

“I don’t have another recovery in me.”

item.title: Help Wanted: ‘Forward-Deployed’ Humans for the A.I. Era
item.description:
The job title “forward-deployed engineer” — someone who works with customers to set up technology, gather feedback and iron out problems — has been around for more than a decade.

But lately, as companies need fewer people to write code, and more people to schlep to client offices to help them integrate new artificial intelligence tools, use of the descriptor for tech roles of all kinds is exploding.

On LinkedIn, job listings for forward-deployed engineers have increased twelvefold in the past year, a company spokeswoman said. And new job titles like forward-deployed product manager, forward-deployed strategist and forward-deployed architect have appeared on the platform, too.

On the job site Indeed, listings seeking forward-deployed engineers jumped 730 percent over the past year. Such openings are rising at a significantly higher rate than other tech jobs, said Sneha Puri, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab — though the raw numbers for these types of listings are still fairly low, in the thousands. The need for this type of support staff, she said, has risen partly because “enterprises are buying A.I. systems, but they don’t necessarily know how to set it up in the best way.”

In a rapidly shifting job landscape, forward-deployed roles are, at least for now, a relatively safe bet, said Nick Bloom, a Stanford economist. A.I. is getting good at many day-to-day work tasks. But forward-deployed workers are responsible for a function that A.I. cannot replace: hands-on client support.

The appeal of this job title — first made popular by Palantir — reflects both reality and hype, Mr. Bloom said. To be sure, someone who can coach a client on integrating a new tool is quite useful right now. But a major factor behind its spread, he noted, is also simply that “it sounds cool.” The title conjures military might — not conference rooms and slide decks.

Companies have an easier time recruiting people into roles that impress their friends and parents, and “forward-deployed engineer sounds to many people a lot better than customer-based engineer,” Mr. Bloom reflected. Versions of these jobs — often with less jazzy titles, like “consultant” — have existed for years. “You are upselling through a title,” he said.

It appears to be working. Not only are people seeking out this role but some are even revising their past job descriptions on LinkedIn, said Mr. Bloom, whose team has been collecting data on how workers edit their job history on that site. Their data shows a sharp uptick this year in changes of titles like software engineer, data engineer and solutions architect to “forward-deployed engineer” (though the overall number of people who have done this is still small, in the hundreds).

The job’s buzz also captures Silicon Valley’s recent embrace, and glorification, of military culture. “Tech companies would probably try to call people ‘Special Ops’ or ‘Delta Force’ if they could get away with it,” Mr. Bloom suggested. Lately, he said, it feels as if companies are copying-and-pasting cool titles from action movies onto job postings. “It’s the ‘Top Gun: Silicon Valley’ generation.”

item.title: The Case of the Truly Incorrigible Cubicle Yakker
item.description:
Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend,

I have a cubicle neighbor who never stops talking. She yells my name over the cubicle wall, or turns the corner and stands at my desk, and proceeds to talk at me for 40 or more minutes at a time. I wish I were exaggerating, but this is a weekly occurrence. There’s simply no way to stop her, or even to ignore her and continue working while she chatters on. Mine is the only other cubicle near hers, so I am her sole victim. Her direct co-workers and supervisors are in another state, and she uses our office as her home base.

Several times now I’ve told her directly, “I have to focus on work and I can’t do that when you’re talking to me.” But she’ll simply start her next “conversation” with, “I know you’re busy and I’m bothering you, but—” and chat for huge chunks of time. I requested noise canceling headphones and have tried ignoring her, but she simply taps me aggressively on the shoulder. I’ve begged my supervisor — who is not her supervisor and who has no power over her — to tell her to leave me alone, because it genuinely affects how much work I get done. I’ve begged to have my desk moved several times. All denied. I have no way to communicate with her supervisor. I’ve run out of ideas.

Please tell me there’s some magical solution that I haven’t thought of!

— Anonymous

It’s remarkable how often the advice I give in this column boils down to something like, “Have you tried speaking directly with the person in your office whose behavior is irritating you in some way?” People’s fear of coming across as rude in the workplace is extraordinarily powerful, and allows them to avoid taking the most obvious steps to fix problems — but it also keeps me in business, so I guess I can’t complain.

But what can I do when someone (you) has already tried this basic default advice, and directly expressed their frustration to the irritating co-worker in question — as well as tried many other things besides? For better or worse, I’m just going to stand firm: I think you need to speak even more directly with this person than you already have.

The fact that your co-worker is this deeply oblivious to your lack of interest in (let alone frustration with) her one-sided conversation suggests to me that she is not a person who picks up well on social cues. At the same time, I suspect you are generally a polite and gentle person. What a socially sensitive person like yourself sees as an almost too-loud-and-clear signal to go away may not even register on her radar.

Which means you may need to turn up the volume (so to speak) much higher than you would normally be comfortable with. For the vast majority of people, “I can’t work when you’re talking to me” is easily understood as an imperative. But a person like this seems to interpret it as a neutral statement of fact. In which case you need to be unmistakably clear.

Have you tried saying some version of, “Please stop talking to me now — I need to return to work?” That kind of directness might help her better understand what you want. If she won’t let you get a word in edgewise, well: Have you tried interrupting her to say it? Have you tried saying it over and over and over, until she stops? Doing this (or something similar) might feel impossibly rude to you — it would to me! — but given the vast difference between your competing understandings of what constitutes polite behavior, I’m not sure your co-worker will interpret it the same way.

Dear Work Friend,

I am a mid-40s nonprofit professional. At nine jobs since graduating college, I’ve experienced two basic kinds of workplaces. In one, I like my team and my supervisors, but the work is mundane, frustrating or unsatisfying. In the other, I am passionate about the work, but my team is terrible.

The latter describes my current role. I love my clients and the work I do has enormous value. But there is no communication, support, clarity, consistency or respect from my supervisors. I get my work done despite my supervisors, not because of them.

Now I have the opportunity to take a new role, one that fits the former description — a fantastic boss and colleague, small office, lots of open communication and collaboration, potential for growth. But it’s highly technical work that doesn’t require creativity, and that puts me in front of a screen, alone, a lot more. Which is worse? Which is better? Which would you choose, and why?

— Anonymous

As much as I would like to rise to the occasion of such a philosophical question with a learned disquisition on the pursuit of work that is consistent, healthy, creative and filled with meaning, the only truthful answer to your question is for me to shrug and say: It depends.

Indeed, I think you already know this, given that you’ve outlined the trade-offs quite clearly, and that you yourself have already switched several times over the course of your career between “mundane but stable” and “satisfying but toxic” jobs. If one was consistently the better option, wouldn’t you, at some point, have elected to stay in that lane?

In some sense I’m surprised you’re even contacting me, as I think you might have figured it out better than anyone. If it’s near-impossible to find both fulfillment and well-being at a single job — and based on the letters I get, I think it is, especially in the nonprofit sector — why not tack between the two, ensuring that over the course of a career, you average out to enviable overall levels of stress, boredom, passion and creativity?

Which is one reason I would suggest, in this instance, to take this new opportunity. You’ve done your time in the “valuable but corrosive” half of the equation recently; time to balance it out with a few years on the “mind-numbing but healthy” side. If you find yourself missing the fulfillment of your current job — and downplaying in your memory the lack of communication and support you received — you know it’s time to switch yet again.

Hi Work Friend,

I recently did the first round of a job interview in which I was on a Microsoft Teams call with five employees of the company, who all kept their cameras off during the entirety of the half-hour call. No explanation was given.

As someone who has never done an interview over Teams before, is this (everyone’s camera off) a common thing? I found it impersonal — not to mention weird and distracting to stare at my own face during the interview.

Should I provide feedback about this strange interview to someone I know who works at the company? She is high up and may not be aware that this is what the staff is doing. I don’t want this to be a sour grapes thing — I didn’t progress to round two — but I honestly would like to spare other potential interviewees a bizarre experience.

— Anonymous

I’m with you on this one. As a practice, camera-off interviews are not at all unheard-of, but they’re also not widely accepted as normal or appropriate. (Reddit and other places where job seekers congregate online are crowded with stories of alienating camera-off interviews.) Your interview, in particular — no heads-up before the meeting, no explanation during it, and not even an opportunity offered to turn your own camera off — sounds particularly egregious. In addition to the general sense that you’re not worth the undivided attention of the hiring panel, there’s something deeply discomfiting and dystopian about watching yourself flop-sweat before the Faceless Microsoft Teams Tribunal.

But even so, I don’t think you should say anything to your contact. You say you don’t want it to sound like sour grapes, but I’m not sure what else it could possibly sound like: You don’t owe this company anything, and “saving hypothetical future interviewees from 30 minutes of awkwardness” is not particularly convincing as a reason to lean on your relationship with a senior figure at the company. If she ever asks, don’t lie, but it’s hard to imagine an outcome worth the risk of burning some good will with this person. Instead, make it a policy to ask before interviews if they’re camera-on or camera-off — and familiarize yourself with the way to hide your own camera view in Teams.

item.title: Dear Borrower, Someone Might Be Stealing Your Home, No Big Deal
item.description:
Welcome back from vacation! Someone may have stolen your home.

That isn’t precisely what the paper letter from PNC Bank, my mortgage servicer, said, but it was close.

It had displayed, in large font, a highlighted exclamation point followed by a foreboding message — “We’re confirming changes to your address” — across the top. The letter went on. “We recently received changes to your address information for your account(s), due to an address change request submitted by you or a joint account holder, either to PNC directly or through the U.S. Postal Service.”

My wife and I had made no such request. But in a world where deed theft — the attempt to literally swipe your property out from under you — is rampant, the letter signaled that thieves might be up to no good.

But were they? It was way harder than it should have been to answer that question.

After checking PNC’s website and seeing no evidence of an address change, I called the 800 number on the letter, as it instructed me to do. In these sorts of instances, it’s best to first make sure that the letter itself is not fake and check that phone number against the company website.

The representative on the phone couldn’t explain the letter, saw no evidence of it in her systems and told me I could disregard it. That wasn’t reassuring, so she told me that I could add a layer of security to my account, but only if I went to a PNC branch.

At 200 Broadway in Manhattan, I encountered Jonathan Villagomez, a patient branch banker. He didn’t know about this supposed heightened security feature, and he made one call and then another to track it down.

During the second call, he passed the phone to me. I spent about 15 minutes with a rep trying to sort it out, and the rep eventually said there actually wasn’t any additional layer of security. The whole branch adventure had been a waste of everyone’s time.

The original rep I spoke to on the phone, before going to the branch, was both right and wrong, according to a PNC spokeswoman I eventually contacted. The bank had sent the letter in error, so it was fine to disregard. Somewhere along the way, something about the absence of our apartment number in one of its records tripped up its systems and led to a belief that someone had changed our address.

But that original rep was wrong that there was any additional available security. We already had two-factor authentication set up (which can keep thieves out of your account if they can’t intercept the code that the bank sends in the moment), and that was going to be the best we could do.

The bank spokeswoman said it was working to ensure that its reps “have clear guidance for addressing questions related to incidents such as this.”

Mistakes are inevitable at big banks with millions of customers. So are the resulting scarygrams like the one we got in the mail, though it’s good that the bank confirms that the address changes it detects are real and intentional. But there was in fact more we could do to protect our deed, and we went ahead and did it.

Many local governmental bodies, including ours, allow you to set up an alert for any changes to your deed. So we did that by going to a New York City website.

A quick search for the name of your town or county and something like “property protection alerts” should lead you there, though be on the lookout for fake government websites. If there are no alerts in your area, ask your elected officials to add them.

Then there’s EquityProtect, which for $149.99 per year will let you in on a process it has developed that can stop deed theft. The company attaches a kind of lock to your title that creates a roadblock for thieves who are trying to sell your property or borrow against it while pretending they are the legitimate owners.

Jon Dovidio, EquityProtect’s vice president of business development, said I was right to send up flares with PNC. He pointed me to a harrowing case in Queens in which the owner of an inherited property got an email from the mortgage servicer about an address change. He contacted the company and discovered that someone had paid off the loan. When he went to the property, he encountered construction workers throwing his childhood photo albums into a dumpster.

I didn’t sign up for EquityProtect and probably won’t for now, so this is not necessarily an endorsement. Deed theft often occurs when criminals take advantage of older owners or target vacant properties where the owner may have recently died and heirs are delayed or distracted. That’s not our situation, but if it was, I’d think hard about whether EquityProtect’s offering was worth it.

You or someone close to you might fit this description, though. If you do, don’t let your paper mail or email pile up. After all, your next letter could be the real thing.
